items.title: An RCD doesn't measure how big the current is — it measures whether currents balance
items.claim: A fuse blows when current rises too high. A residual current device (RCD or ground-fault circuit interrupter) does something different: it measures the difference between current going OUT on the live wire and current returning on the neutral. Any imbalance over about 30 mA trips the device in 25 ms.
items.prompt: Why measure imbalance rather than total current?

options.text: In a healthy circuit, current out equals current back. If any current is leaking to earth (through a person, a faulty appliance, water in a socket), the two no longer balance — and that's exactly the dangerous condition a fuse can't detect

items.reveal:
The live and neutral wires both pass through a small toroidal core inside the RCD. If equal current flows in opposite directions, their magnetic fields cancel exactly — no signal. If a fraction leaks to earth (say, through a person touching a live wire), the currents no longer cancel and a net magnetic flux is induced through the core.

A small sensing coil picks up the imbalance and triggers a fast electromechanical switch. UK regulations require trip thresholds of 30 mA or less and trip times under 40 ms for socket circuits in dwellings.

Fuses protect against the wires overheating (overcurrent); RCDs protect against the person being electrocuted (earth leakage). Modern installations combine them as RCBOs.
items.why: Safety devices are taught as 'fuses prevent fires'. RCDs and earth wires together prevent the more common cause of injury — leakage current through a human body.

items.title: Devices on standby cost the world about 1 percent of total electricity
items.claim: TVs, set-top boxes, microwaves, phone chargers and printers continue to draw current even when 'off'. The International Energy Agency estimated this 'phantom load' or 'vampire power' at about 1 percent of global electricity consumption — roughly 250 TWh per year.
items.prompt: Why does a device draw power when you've turned it off?

options.text: The device keeps a remote-control receiver, clock, memory or network interface powered — typically through a small transformer that wastes a few watts continuously
Electricity meters are inaccurate at low currents
Heat from the wires keeps the device warm

items.reveal:
A typical TV on standby draws 1-5 W. A printer 2-10 W. A microwave with a clock 1-3 W. Phone chargers without a phone 0.1-1 W. A wifi router can draw 5-15 W around the clock.

Average UK household has 15-20 always-on devices. Total standby load can reach 50-100 W continuously — about 500-1000 kWh per year, costing £100-200.

EU regulations now cap standby consumption: most products must use under 0.5 W in standby. Newer designs use 'soft-off' switches that genuinely cut almost all current. The simplest fix is unplugging or using switched extension leads.
items.why: 'Off' is not zero. Small persistent loads multiplied by billions of devices add up to a percentage of global energy use.
